turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re diving into this! Let me break the main options down really simply.

First choice: what kind of plant?
Roses: Our specialty. All are own-root in 1-gallon containers, grown in soil.
Perennials: Companion plants like lavender, salvia, catmint, etc. that come back every year.
Bulbs: Tulips, daffodils, crocus, etc., planted in fall for spring blooms.
Soil & fertilizer: Compost, manure, and rose food to help everything grow better.

Most people start with roses, then add a few perennials around them.

For roses: the main style choices

Think about how you want the rose to look and act in your garden:

Climbing roses
Grow tall on arches, fences, or trellises. Great if you want a big vertical display.

Shrub / bush roses
Rounded shape, good for most gardens and borders. Many are very full and “English garden” looking.

Hybrid tea roses
Classic long stems with one big bloom per stem. Best if you dream of cutting roses for vases.

Groundcover / landscape roses
Lower, spreading habit. Good for edging, slopes, or filling in space.

Practical things to decide
Sun: Roses need full sun (6+ hours of direct sun a day) to really do well.
Hardiness zone: This is about winter cold. At the top of our website you can pick your zone so you only see plants that can live in your climate.
Size: Product pages list height and width in feet, so you know how big the rose will get.
Fragrance: Some are lightly scented, some are very strong. You can filter for fragrance on the site.
Bloom style:
Repeat or continuous blooming: flowers come in waves through the season.
Once-blooming: a big, beautiful show once a year (less common in modern garden choices).
How to browse easily on our site
Go to “Shop All Roses” at the top of the page.
At the top, set your hardiness zone so you only see roses that can thrive where you live.
Use filters on the left side for:
Type (climbing, shrub, hybrid tea, etc.)

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. You don’t need a ton of stuff to start, just a few helpful basics.

Here’s what I recommend for a beginner:

Helpful add-ons for planting

If you want a “one and done” starter set, our Get Growing Bundle is a really easy choice. It combines our favorite amendments so you don’t have to figure it all out piece by piece.

If you prefer to keep it even simpler, the two most useful items are:

Mint compost
Mixed into your planting hole, it helps improve soil, retain moisture, and protect roots.

Fish fertilizer (Founders Fish Fertilizer)
A gentle fertilizer you can use every 4 weeks during the growing season to support healthy growth in that first year.

All of these are optional, but they really help your rose establish nicely and handle less-than-perfect conditions.

A couple of basic tools/steps

Aside from the rose and amendments, you really just need:

A shovel for digging a wide planting hole
Good quality garden soil or compost if your native soil is very hard or sandy
Access to water (consistent deep watering, especially the first season)
At least 6 hours of direct sun in the spot you choose

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and good on you for wanting to do it right from day one.

Since you’re a beginner, here’s a very simple way to use the Get Growing Bundle the first time.

I’ll split it into two parts so you can follow the one that fits you:

If you’re planting in the ground
Dig the hole
Dig about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep so the roots have room.
Add aged cow manure
Put a few inches of your native soil in the bottom.
Add a layer of the aged cow manure on top of that bottom soil.
Mix in bone meal
In a bucket or wheelbarrow, mix the topsoil from the hole with about 1 cup of bone meal.
Put this mixed soil back into the hole around where the rose roots will sit.
Add the rose and mint compost
Place the rose so the base of the plant is at ground level.
Backfill with your soil/bone meal mix.
Spread the mint compost on top of the soil around the rose as a “top layer” (mulch). This helps keep moisture in and protects roots.
Water with fish fertilizer
Mix Founders Fish Fertilizer: about 4 oz per gallon of water (check the label too).
Water the rose deeply with this mix after planting.
Then repeat the fish fertilizer every 4–6 weeks during the growing season.
If you’re planting in a container
Choose the right pot
For a rose: at least 10–15 gallons for a bush type.
Make sure there are drainage holes.
Mix the soil and cow manure
In a tub or wheelbarrow, mix your potting soil (without granular fertilizer) with some aged cow manure.
Fill the pot most of the way with this mix.
Add bone meal
Mix about 1 cup of bone meal into the soil in the planting area of the pot.
Plant the rose and top with mint compost
Place the rose so the base is at the final soil level.
Fill in around the roots with your soil mix.
Add mint compost on top of the soil around the base as a thin layer.
Water with fish fertilizer
Mix 4 oz of Founders Fish Fertilizer per gallon of water.
Water the rose thoroughly after planting.
Repeat every 3–4 weeks during the growing season.

That’s it for a good first use: manure and bone meal in the planting mix, mint compost on top, fish fertilizer in the water.
